titre: The Phonautograph: A Recording Made to Be Read
accroche: In 1860, a Parisian typesetter has a machine that cannot play anything back sing “Au clair de la lune.” It will take nearly 150 years to hear it.
contenu_vulgarise:
On April 9, 1860, in Paris, someone sings the first words of “Au clair de la lune” into the horn of a device. At the back, a membrane vibrates and drives a stylus that scratches a sheet covered in lampblack. The machine has no loudspeaker and no means of reading back what it has just written. It produces only a wavy line some twenty seconds long. That line is today the oldest intelligible recording of a human voice.

## Photographing speech

The inventor, Édouard-Léon Scott de Martinville (1817-1879), is neither a physicist nor an engineer: he is a typesetter and manuscript proofreader at a Parisian scientific publishing house. In 1853 or 1854, reading a physiology treatise describing the ear, he has what he calls “the imprudent idea of photographing speech”: if the eye can be copied by a photographic apparatus, a copy of the ear should be able to fix the voice. He obtains a patent in 1857 and names his machine the phonautograph, that is, “the self-writing of sound.” Supported by the Society for the Encouragement of National Industry, he turns it into a laboratory instrument that scientists adopt at the end of 1857. To measure time on the tracing, he has a tuning fork write next to the voice: each oscillation, at a known frequency, serves as a graduation.

The decisive point is that Scott is not trying to play these tracings back. He intends them to be read: he hopes people will learn to decipher these undulations as a kind of natural shorthand. No one at the time conceives of hearing a recording. The idea only appears in mid-1877, almost simultaneously with Charles Cros in France, who sketches his paleophone, and with Thomas Edison in the United States, who begins his phonograph.

## Listening, one hundred forty-eight years later

Scott's tracings survived in Parisian archives. In 2008, the First Sounds group and American researchers, including those at the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, digitized the paper by optical scanning and translated the undulations into sound by computer, without damaging the original. The result was first played at twice the right speed: it sounded like a woman or a child. In 2009, the team noticed that another tracing from the same series, a recitation in Italian, sounded like the Chipmunks at that speed. Brought back to the right pace, “Au clair de la lune” is sung very slowly by a man, almost certainly Scott himself.

## What this shifts

It is often repeated that Edison invented sound recording in 1877. Scott's tracings show a different story: sound was fixed seventeen years earlier, and what was missing was reading by ear. The question “what is the first recording?” therefore depends on a definition. Does a tracing that no one could listen to for nearly a century and a half count as a recording, or only as a writing? According to First Sounds, six collections hold several dozen of these recordings made in Paris between about 1853 and 1860, of which only about twenty have been made audible. The rest is waiting to be looked at, at last, as sound.

repere.texte: On April 9, 1860, Scott de Martinville records “Au clair de la lune” on his phonautograph, seventeen years before Edison's phonograph. The tracing is only converted into sound in 2008, nearly one hundred fifty years later.

quiz.question: Why couldn't Scott de Martinville listen to his recordings again?
choix: The tracings on blackened paper smudged as soon as they were touched with a stylus
He meant them to be read by eye, and the idea of playing them back did not yet exist
The device only engraved sounds too low for a machine to play back
He had destroyed his tracings after presenting them to the Society for the Encouragement of National Industry
quiz.explication: The machine had no means of playback: Scott wanted the tracings to be deciphered like shorthand, and the idea of hearing them only appears in 1877. The tracings did not smudge (they were read in 2008), were not limited to low sounds, and were not destroyed: they slept in Parisian archives.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What made it possible to understand, in 2009, that the 1860 recording had first been played at the wrong speed?
choix: The volume of the tuning fork inscribed on the tracing, which no longer matched its known frequency
Another tracing from the same series, a recitation in Italian, which sounded like the Chipmunks at that speed
A second phonautograph found in the archives, calibrated at the right speed
Scott de Martinville's written testimony, found in his personal notebooks
quiz_supplementaire.explication: On finding a recitation in Italian from the same collection that, played at the same speed as “Au clair de la lune,” sounded like the Chipmunks, the team understood that the initial playback speed was wrong and corrected the rendering in 2009.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Before the 1860 recording, what had already made the phonautograph an instrument used by people other than its inventor?
choix: A partnership with Thomas Edison, who financed its mass production
Its adoption by the Academy of Sciences as the official instrument for measuring time
The marketing of the phonautograph as a toy for Parisian salons
The support of the Society for the Encouragement of National Industry, adopted by scientists as early as late 1857
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text places the institutional support before the 1860 recording: the Society for the Encouragement of National Industry made the phonautograph a laboratory instrument adopted by scientists as early as the end of 1857.
